thread.title: When Apple ( AAPL ) held its conference call for the FQ1 ear

author: J. M. Manness
title: When Apple ( AAPL ) held its conference call for the FQ1 ear
text:
When Apple ( AAPL ) held its conference call for the FQ1 earnings release, CFO Luca Maestri made some very important comments relating to the company’s enormous cash position. He said:
Tax reform will allow us to pursue a more optimal capital structure for our company. Our current net cash position is $163 billion. And given the increased financial and operational flexibility from the access to our foreign cash, we are targeting to become approximately net cash neutral over time.
In a previous post I discussed how FQ1 earnings results were really much better than most analysts have recognized. That is, when you account for the extra week a year ago, Apple handily beat year-over-year numbers in both revenue and unit sales . In a follow up post, I discussed the real implications of Apple’s revenue guidance , including an estimation of iPhone sales.
In this post I will discuss the importance of the impending repatriation of Apple’s overseas cash hoard.
How much? As noted in the above quote, Apple is sitting on about $163 billion in net cash and marketable securities, after subtracting debt. It will also cost in taxes to repatriate this amount from overseas. One estimate is $38 billion.
Since cash generates quickly overseas, we can expect the company will repatriate virtually all of it. This will give us some $125 billion to work with more or less immediately.
How will it be used? Acquisitions 
Obviously, speculation abounds on the use of this cash. Some believe that Apple is in line for some very large acquisitions. To my mind, however, this is very unlikely, for several reasons, both related to core values.
First, Apple does not exist to grow, nor to maximize share price. The motivation for Apple (and I imagine many long-term investors as well) is to create the best possible products, incorporating quality at every level of design. It is the manic dedication to this goal that has led it to become the largest (market cap) and most influential company on the planet today.
Second, and related – possibly a corollary of the first, is the often noted dedication to producing just a few products so that the team can focus intently on them. Jony Ive is quoted :
The discipline to turn your back on something you believe in passionately so you can apply yourself to what’s at hand is really remarkable. It’s a deeply uncomfortable but really effective thing to do.
“(Jobs) would try to help me improve my focus by asking me, ‘How many times did you say no today?'”
This is, as Tim Cook likes to say, “embedded in Apple’s DNA.”
Finally, historic acquisitions by Apple have been smaller companies with very targeted key technologies. This is likely to continue.
Dividends 
Again, speculation abounds. Apple already gives a dividend. Clearly, some proportion of Apple’s cash will go to this. While some people would like to see either a dramatic rise in the dividends or some grand special (one-time) dividend of several dollars, again, to my mind this is unlikely.
Here are Apple's statistics from the Yahoo Finance page.

Two things to note:
The dividend yield of roughly 1.45% (both forward and trailing) The payout ratio is about 25% Both of these figures are low, at least in terms of desirable dividend stocks. But No. 2 in particular shows that Apple could very easily double the dividend and still have a relatively low payout ratio. In fact, quadrupling the dividend would give a sustainable dividend and an enviable yield. It undoubtedly would drive the price up drastically, as many would like.
Once again, however, Apple does not exist to please the investor. Its focus is on delivering to customers the best product possible on many different levels. It is a lesson to others how if you focus on this in the long run you will give the best return to investors.
So quadrupling dividends or a large special dividend is unlikely. 
Share Repurchase 
A year ago I wrote in detail why money spent on repurchases is equivalent to dividends , even better in the long run if earnings keep increasing. I calculated the “ real dividend yield .”
Apple has been buying back shares for several years now. This has reduced the number of shares to the point that it has a very significant effect on EPS. As most of you understand, earnings for a given quarter are a real world given, but if you have fewer total shares, then the earnings per each share is greater. There are fewer slices in the proverbial (apple) pie, so each is larger.
In fact, a large proportion of EPS growth over the last few years is due to reduction in share count. This last quarter (FQ1 2018) had almost $1 greater EPS than if there were still 6.63 billion shares as there were in 2012 calendar Q4.
The chart below shows how share count has declined. (Note – share count is on a different scale than the other lines. Values run from roughly 6.7 down to 5.2 billion shares.)
The blue line is the dollar difference between a given quarter’s EPS and what it would have been if there still were 6.63 billion shares. (This ignores the fact that shares also are being created for employee options, etc., and some of the buyback has canceled this. Realistically the comparison should actually be increasing from 6.63 B.)
The green line is the same (difference) but as a percentage of overall EPS. One should note how it is increasing steadily.

The data show that this past quarter 86.7 cents of the $3.89 EPS was due to decreased share count.
Why buybacks? 
There are several reasons Apple directors prefer buybacks.
One, I believe they feel that Apple is undervalued by the market, and so buying shares is the best value for the investor.
Second, Steve Jobs was not fond of analysts and speculators, and this legacy carries on. To Apple leaders, if you simply give the money away (in dividends) then it is gone. Repurchases are the “gift that keeps giving,” and as such favor long-term investors . These are the investors Apple likes – ones who believe in the company overall, who are in it for the long haul.
I imagine there may be other reasons as well.
The solution So what is the likely outcome?
My guess is as follows.
We should keep in mind what was expressed in the conference call -that debts are paid off or balanced by cash and equivalents, and there's only a modest reserve above this. Thus, Apple is dedicated to spending almost all the cash.
Repurchases –
Apple will spend virtually all the reclaimed $163 billion on repurchases over the next two to four years. I believe they will even fund the $38 billion tax payment from future profits. Dividends – 
Apple can easily fund dividends from quarterly earnings and still have several billion per quarter left over. 
Dividends will be funded from quarterly earnings, not directly from repatriated cash. I think it likely that they will double the dividend, perhaps over two years. Currently, the dividend is at $0.63. They can boost that in April to about $1, perhaps a bit under, say $0.94. They don’t want to spike the share price too much, as this would damage the buying power of the repurchase program. 
Bottom line The repatriation money, assuming no extraordinary acquisitions , will most likely be used for repurchases. This is in line with previous behavior.
If Apple spends $160 billion on repurchases, and the average price paid is $200, then that would retire 800 million shares, bringing the total down to roughly 4.2 billion.
If this had been done on December 30 last year, with FQ1 earnings of $20 billion, the EPS would have been $4.76 instead of $3.89. This is the kind of effect it would have going forward: 
a 22% rise in EPS. Summary Obviously, there's a lot of speculation here. Only the top key people at Apple know for certain what exactly is their plan and how it will play out. Furthermore, realistically speaking, such a plan, along with future growth, will almost assuredly the lift share price well over $200. My guess is that to spend just the $163 billion repatriated cash will take at least 10 quarters, or two and a half years.
Yet the fact remains, the words of Luca Maestri (the official voice of Apple, Inc.) are clear:
We are targeting to become approximately net cash neutral over time. This is unequivocal. The directors are going to work down the cash position close to net zero. They have to do this someway, and they have shown their preference is for share repurchases.
A final note: 
Yesterday, Apple closed at $171.07. Yahoo lists TTM earnings at $9.70. Add 22% and you get $11.43. Currently the PE is 17.64 – let's say 18. Adding the 22% (as if Apple could magically buy share with cash tomorrow) this would give a share price of $213. 
The question is simple. 
If Apple is worth a PE of 18, and the cash position is worth 22%, then why is Apple not worth $213 today? Your comments are appreciated.
